subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The EV Startup Graveyard
description: A quick, practical guide to The EV Startup Graveyard.

hook.text: Hundreds of EV startups launched in the 2020s. Most of them are already dead or dying.

buildup.text: Lordstown, Fisker, Arrival, Faraday Future—all raised billions, all collapsed before reaching scale.

discovery.text: Building cars is incredibly capital-intensive. You need factories, supply chains, and service networks.

twist.text: Rivian survived by securing Amazon delivery van orders. Lucid survived by Saudi funding.

climax.text: The lesson: making a great prototype is easy. Mass production is where startups die.

quiz.question: Why do most EV startups fail?

details.summary: Dozens of EV startups including Fisker, Lordstown Motors, and Arrival collapsed after burning through billions, proving that designing an electric car is far easier than manufacturing and selling one profitably.
details.whyItMatters: The EV startup graveyard shows that automotive manufacturing is brutally capital-intensive. Even promising technology cannot overcome the challenges of mass production, supply chains, and distribution.
takeaways: Fisker, Lordstown, and Arrival all filed for bankruptcy
Manufacturing at scale remains the hardest challenge for startups
Rivian and Lucid survive but continue burning cash heavily

faq.question: Why do so many EV startups fail?
faq.answer: Car manufacturing requires enormous capital, complex supply chains, and regulatory compliance that most startups underestimate. Reaching profitable production volumes takes years and billions more than initial projections typically assume.

faq.question: Which EV startups might still succeed?
faq.answer: Rivian has Amazon's backing and actual production at scale. Lucid has Saudi investment and a competitive luxury product. Both are still unprofitable but have the resources and product quality to potentially survive long-term.
